schemaVersion: Ehel Level 2 Intensive English Placement Exam v1.0
subject: Intensive English
title: Level 2 English Placement Exam
description: A check of the English Level 1 builds: the everyday words, the sentence patterns from am and is through to the past and comparing, and reading a short note or a set of instructions. It is not a test you can fail — it finds the right place for you to start.
attemptsAllowed: Unlimited — this exam finds your starting point; it is never a fail
feedbackMode: Immediate supportive feedback with a placement report

readyWithReview.message: You are ready to begin Level 2. Warm up first with the Level 1 units below — an hour with them will make the new work feel lighter.

notReady.label: Let's build your foundations first
notReady.message: Your English will grow fastest on a strong foundation. Start with Level 1 — it begins with the letters and their sounds and moves at your pace, and this exam will be here whenever you are ready to try again.

sections.title: Everyday words
sections.description: The words Level 1 built for the room and the kitchen, the town, jobs, travel, prices and how people are.

remediation.title: Numbers to 100, and How Things Are

sections.title: Sentence patterns
sections.description: The patterns from Level 1 — am, is and are, there is and there are, what is happening now, the past, asking, comparing, and writing a sentence properly.

sections.title: Reading and talking to people
sections.description: Short everyday texts — a set of instructions, directions, a message — and the words that keep a conversation going.

questions.question: Which of these do you sit on?
questions.options: a chair | a shelf | a window | a wall
questions.explanation: You sit on a chair. A shelf is the tempting one because things rest on it — but things rest on a shelf, people do not sit on it.

questions.question: It is raining. Which thing do you take with you?
questions.options: a pencil | a photo | an umbrella | a bottle
questions.explanation: An umbrella keeps the rain off you. A bottle is the easy mistake because it holds water — but you carry water in a bottle, you do not keep rain off with one.

questions.question: You want to cut the meat on your plate. Which one do you use?
questions.options: a spoon | a knife | a bowl | a fork
questions.explanation: A knife cuts. A fork is the close one because it is in your other hand at the same time — but a fork holds the meat, it does not cut it.

questions.question: You are reading and you do not know what a word means. Which book do you open?
questions.options: a postcard | a notebook | a story | a dictionary
questions.explanation: A dictionary tells you what a word means. A notebook is the tempting one because you write new words in it — but you put words into a notebook, and you take their meaning out of a dictionary.

questions.question: The price of a bag in the market is 20. The price of the same bag in the shop is 50. The bag in the market is ______.
questions.options: cheap | expensive | heavy | busy
questions.explanation: Cheap means the price is low. Expensive is the opposite and is the easy mistake here — 50 is the expensive one, 20 is the cheap one.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Numbers to 100, and How Things Are

questions.question: Your neighbour helps other people every day. Which word describes her?
questions.options: busy | tall | kind | young
questions.explanation: Kind describes how a person is to other people. Busy is the tempting one because somebody who helps all day has a lot to do — but busy says how much work she has, not how she treats people.
questions.sourceUnitTitle: Numbers to 100, and How Things Are

questions.question: Where do you go to borrow a book and bring it back later?
questions.options: the bank | the library | the market | the cinema
questions.explanation: A library lends you books and you bring them back. The market is where people go for things they keep — at a library the book is only yours for a time.

questions.question: You did not eat in the morning and you did not eat at lunch. How do you feel now?
questions.options: angry | thirsty | tired | hungry
questions.explanation: Hungry is the word for wanting food. Thirsty is the near one and is about drink, not food — you say thirsty when you want water.

questions.question: A woman works with the doctor at the hospital and helps the people there. What is her job?
questions.options: a cleaner | a nurse | a farmer | a driver
questions.explanation: A nurse works with the doctor and looks after people. A cleaner is the tempting one because cleaners work at a hospital too — but a cleaner cleans the building, and a nurse cares for the people.

questions.question: The road is not safe at night. Which word means the same as 'not safe'?
questions.options: comfortable | different | dangerous | difficult
questions.explanation: Dangerous is the opposite of safe, so 'not safe' and 'dangerous' say the same thing. Difficult is the close one — a difficult road is hard to drive on, but that is not the same as hurting you.

questions.question: You want to travel by train. Where do you wait for it?
questions.options: at the station | at the corner | at the bridge | at the beach
questions.explanation: Trains stop at a station, and that is where you wait. A corner is the tempting one because you do wait at a corner — but that is for a taxi or a bus in the street, not for a train.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'My brother and I ______ from the same city.'
questions.options: is | am | be | are
questions.explanation: My brother and I means we, and we takes are. Am is the tempting one because the word I is in the sentence — but I is only half of the subject here, and two people together always take are.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.options: There is three chairs in the office. | There are three chairs in the office. | There are three chair in the office. | It has three chairs in the office.
questions.correctAnswer: There are three chairs in the office.
questions.explanation: Three chairs is more than one, so both the verb and the noun are plural: there are, three chairs. 'There is three chairs' is the common slip — is belongs with one thing only: there is a chair.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'Please wait — she ______ on the phone at the moment.'
questions.options: talk | talks | is talking | talking
questions.explanation: At the moment means right now, so use is plus the -ing form: she is talking. Talks is the tempting one — she talks on the phone is a habit, something she does often, not something happening as you wait.

questions.question: Choose the sentence with 'always' in the correct place.
questions.options: I always take the bus to work. | I take always the bus to work. | I am always take the bus to work. | I take the bus to always work.
questions.correctAnswer: I always take the bus to work.
questions.explanation: Always, usually, often and never go in front of the main verb: I always take, she never forgets. 'I take always the bus' is the usual mistake, because in many languages the word does come after the verb — in English it does not.

questions.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday I ______ my key at the office.'
questions.options: lose | losing | losed | lost
questions.explanation: Yesterday tells you the action is finished, so you need the past: lost. Losed is the tempting one because most past forms add -ed — but lose is irregular, and its past is lost.

questions.question: You want to use your neighbour's phone. What do you say?
questions.options: I use your phone. | Can I use your phone, please? | Do I use your phone? | Give me your phone.
questions.correctAnswer: Can I use your phone, please?
questions.explanation: Can I is how you ask permission, and please makes it warm. 'Give me your phone' is the one to avoid: it is an order, not a question, and it sounds hard even when you do not mean it to.

questions.question: You have not visited the sea. Choose the correct sentence.
questions.options: I never been to the sea. | I am never been to the sea. | I have never been to the sea. | I have never go to the sea.
questions.correctAnswer: I have never been to the sea.
questions.explanation: For something that has not happened at any time up to now, use have plus been: I have never been. 'I never been to the sea' is the near miss — the have is not extra, it is the word that carries the meaning.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.options: This bag is cheaper than that one. | This bag is more cheap than that one. | This bag is more cheaper than that one. | This bag is cheap than that one.
questions.correctAnswer: This bag is cheaper than that one.
questions.explanation: Short words take -er: cheaper, larger, older. 'More cheap' is the tempting one because more is right for long words — more expensive, more comfortable — but never for a short one, and never both at once.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'I went to the bank ______ pay for my ticket.'
questions.options: for | because | and | to
questions.explanation: To plus a verb gives the purpose — why you went: to pay, to ask, to work. For is the common slip; for takes a noun, so 'for my ticket' is fine but 'for pay' is not.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that is written correctly.
questions.options: my class starts on monday | My class starts on Monday. | My class starts on monday. | my Class starts on Monday.
questions.explanation: A sentence opens with a capital letter, the days of the week keep theirs, and a full stop closes it. 'My class starts on monday.' is the near miss — the sentence is right but the day has lost its capital, and in English every day of the week keeps one.

questions.question: Read the instructions: 'First, cut the vegetables. Next, heat the water. After that, add the rice.' What do you do second?
questions.options: Cut the vegetables. | Add the rice. | Heat the water. | Eat the rice.
questions.explanation: First, next and after that give you the order, and next marks the second step. Cutting the vegetables is the tempting answer because it is the step you notice first — but the question asks for the second one.

questions.question: You ask a woman how to get to the bank. She says: 'Go straight on, cross the road at the traffic lights, and the bank is on your left.' Where is the bank?
questions.options: After the traffic lights, on the left. | Before the traffic lights, on the left. | After the traffic lights, on the right. | At the traffic lights, on the right.
questions.correctAnswer: After the traffic lights, on the left.
questions.explanation: You cross at the traffic lights and the bank comes after that, on your left. 'Before the traffic lights' is the easy mistake — the crossing happens first, so everything the woman says after it is further along the road.

questions.question: Read the message: 'The class starts at six thirty on Thursday.' When is the class?
questions.options: On Tuesday at six thirty. | On Thursday at six o'clock. | On Thursday at seven thirty. | On Thursday at six thirty.
questions.explanation: The message gives you a day and a time, and both must match: Thursday, six thirty. 'On Thursday at six o'clock' is the one that catches people — the day is right, so it looks right, but thirty minutes have been dropped.

questions.question: Someone at work asks you: 'Do you work on Saturdays?' You do not. Which answer is correct?
questions.options: No, I am not. | No, I don't. | No, I doesn't. | No, I not work.
questions.explanation: A question that starts with do is answered with do: Do you work? No, I don't. 'No, I am not' is the usual slip — am and are answer questions that begin with are you or is she, not with do.

questions.question: The doctor speaks quickly and you do not understand. What is the best thing to say?
questions.options: Yes, thank you. | I understand everything. | Please say it again, slowly. | I am sorry, goodbye.
questions.explanation: Asking somebody to say it again, more slowly, is a skill, not a weakness — and most people are glad to help. 'Yes, thank you' is the tempting one because it is polite and quick, but it ends the conversation while you still do not know what was said.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'I wanted the blue bag, ______ it was very expensive.'
questions.options: but | and | or | because
questions.explanation: But joins two ideas that work against each other: you wanted it, and the price stopped you. Because is the tempting one, but it would say the price was the reason you wanted the bag, which turns the sentence around.

questions.question: Read: 'Ana works at the hospital. Last week she had a small accident and she did not work for three days. Next month she will start a new job.' What happened last week?
questions.options: She went to a party. | She started a new job. | She worked for three days. | She had an accident.
questions.explanation: Last week points to the past, and had tells you what happened then. 'She started a new job' is the trap — the new job is in the text, but will start puts it in the future, next month.

questions.question: Read the message: 'I will be late. The bus did not come. See you at seven.' What is the person doing?
questions.options: Asking you to come at six. | Saying they will arrive late. | Asking for a ticket. | Telling you the bus is early.
questions.explanation: I will be late, and the reason follows: the bus did not come. 'Telling you the bus is early' is the near miss — the bus is in the message, but did not come is the opposite of early.

questions.question: You are in a shop. The bag you are looking at is very big and you want a smaller one. What is the best thing to say?
questions.options: Give me a small one. | I want small. | Can I see a smaller one, please? | This one is small.
questions.correctAnswer: Can I see a smaller one, please?
questions.explanation: Can I see, plus please, asks for what you want and keeps the shopkeeper on your side. 'Give me a small one' is the tempting one because the words are easy — but it is an order rather than a request, and one is a small one while the other is a smaller one.
